articles.title: A very serious collection of fabulously fake jewelry
articles.summary: Italian contemporary art collector, Patrizia Sandretto Re Rebaudengo, unveils her vast collection of 20th century American costume jewelry.
articles.body: Patrizia Sandretto Re Rebaudengo takes a somewhat unorthodox approach to getting dressed. Led by her impressive collection of 20th century American costume jewelry, the Italian contemporary art collector begins at the earlobes, the neck, or the wrist, working outwards from there. For important events, Sandretto Re Rebaudengo enlists her regular tailor to make dresses from scratch to ensure they perfectly complement a 1970’s William de Lillo bib of gleaming red, green and blue stones, for example, or a decadent web of Miriam Haskell faux pearls. “We enjoy finding the particular fabric and matching together the jewelry and the dress,” Sandretto Re Rebaudengo said in a video call from her ornate home in Turin, Italy (her other home, in Venice, was designed by film director Luca Guadagnino). “The dress is like a canvas on which I do my drawing… I don’t draw, but I put a brooch on.” The art patron and private museum owner is better known in cultural circles for founding the Fondazione Sandretto Re Rebaudengo in 1995, a contemporary arts institution now with outposts in Turin, Guarene and Venice. But her costume jewelry collection predates even this legacy. Sandretto Re Rebaudengo started buying pieces in the late 1980s, when jewels would cost her as little as $10. Today she owns more than 1,000 brooches, necklaces, bracelets and earrings — each one of them American, the earliest dating back to roughly 1929. The pieces have been exhibited, immortalized in their own coffee table book and most importantly, worn by Rebaudengo herself over and over again. There are no carats in costume jewelry, but that doesn’t dim the shine for Sandretto Re Rebaudengo. “I’ve never been interested in real jewelry,” she said. Instead, she’s curious about the economic forces that gave way to this plug-and-play variety of adornment. Before the Great Depression and the metal shortages of World War II, the jewelry industry had a predominantly male customer base. Women couldn’t afford to buy pieces for themselves, meaning they often had to wait to receive them as gifts from fathers, husbands, lovers or brothers and rarely got the chance to choose according to their own style. But during the war, restricted materials like gold and silver were replaced with pewter, brass and copper — or even more fascinatingly, wood and Bakelite — making jewelry more affordable. “I really believe these are democratic objects,” Sandretto Re Rebaudengo said. “Because finally with a few dollars every woman could go into a shop and buy a necklace or a brooch that she loved with her money.” These were not simple imitations of precious stones, either. De Lillo — one of Sandretto Re Rebaudengo’s most collected designers with over 100 pieces to her name — spent years at Cartier, Tiffany & Co. and Harry Winston before defecting to ‘fake’ jewels and setting up his own company in 1968 with jewelry designer Robert Clark. What emerged were singular styles: playful and gaudy and eccentric, like cascading gold necklaces inspired by Egyptian Pharaohs, bejeweled geometric collars as big as a 16th century ruff or enormous scarab brooches festooned with gems. De Lillo and Clark eventually made pieces for Schiaparelli and Nina Rici, while Haskell’s most important client was Coco Chanel. Today, luxury fashion houses are returning to the maximalist proportion of costume jewels — Matthieu Blazy’s flower pom-pom earrings for Chanel, for example, or Saint Laurent’s Catholic kitsch clip-ons in enamel and glass. But Sandretto Re Rebaudengo wasn’t much interested in fashion history. Instead, she sees these pieces as independent “works of art” that also act as a dazzling map of US history. De Lillo was Belgian, Haskell was Russian and Gustavo Trifari, who launched Trifari in 1910, was Italian. But they all emigrated to the US before starting their businesses. “Through these jewels you can really trace the history of the United States for the past century,” she said. There’s the Trifari ‘Jelly Belly’ brooch series, one of Sandretto Re Rebaudengo’s beloved sub-collections. She holds to the camera a succession of small animals whose trunks are made from a type of aviation-grade acrylic originally used in World War II cockpit windows, canopies and windshields. Then there are the jolly Christmas tree brooches families sent to American soldiers fighting in the Korean War, and the wave of red-white-and-blue patriotic pins that became fashionable during the early 1940s. Collecting is “in my DNA,” said Sandretto Re Rebaudengo. As a child she gathered small decorative pill boxes from markets and antique shops with her mother, then came her brooches and jewels and later, a career in contemporary art collection. The process of buying a work for her Fondazione and a piece for her costume jewellery collection is similar, she said. “It’s always important to buy with my heart, but I also buy in a very precise way.” She researches time periods, designers and inspects the small changes in typeface and brand logos to identify exactly when something was made. “You have to pay attention that all the gems or the stones are from the right period,” she said. “If just one small stone has been changed, it’s not of the same period. The object is not the same.” In many ways, costume jewelry was an early opportunity for women to realize their own taste and preference. Sandretto Re Rebaudengo specifically has crafted a distinct image for herself in a public role. In her early years, she reached for more brooches to pair with her pants and jackets. Today, she skews more towards the working formula of a loud dress and bib-necklace. Pieces in her collection range from $10 to $1,000, though she dodges the question of how much she has spent altogether. “The value is in the object, not so much in the price,” she said. During our interview she tries on a more recent acquisition by one of the few costume jewelery designers still alive today, Billy Boy. An imposing jewel-encrusted dagger hangs from the center of what looks like the Order of the Golden Fleece, the blade even dripping with a little painted blood like something you might see in “Excalibur” (1981). It’s a gem, even in Sandretto Re Rebaudengo’s collection of gems. But what possible occasion could you wear such an extravagant, if not slightly bewildering, piece? Halloween? “Maybe when I have a dinner to go to… Or a party,” she said with a shrug. “I’ll wear this with a black dress.” Clearly Sandretto Re Rebaudengo does not wait to wear her Sunday best, or bloodiest. It does give off a “particular energy” she admits, and to demonstrate quickly shouts with mock indignation, “Pay attention!” It’s true, the glittering faux sword adds weight — and glamour — to a stern word.

articles.title: USS Roosevelt arrives in Middle East: Is the US-Iran war about to resume?
articles.summary: The aircraft carrier joins two others operating in the US Central Command area of responsibility.
articles.body:
The United States has deployed a third aircraft carrier to the Middle East as diplomatic efforts to permanently end the US-Israel war on Iran and reopen the Strait of Hormuz remain stalled.

On Monday, a US official told Al Jazeera that the USS Theodore Roosevelt had arrived in the Middle East. The aircraft carrier joins two others operating in the US Central Command (CENTCOM) area of responsibility.

The US and Iran entered into a two-week ceasefire in April and later announced a broader memorandum of understanding in June, which collapsed in early July.

Since then, mediators from Pakistan and Qatar have been trying to prevent a return to the full-scale exchange of attacks between the US and Iran that also badly affected the broader Gulf region in March.

Last week, US President Donald Trump stated that further military strikes against Iran are “quite unlikely” and said the military component of the war was “effectively over” following discussions with Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani. But he noted the US military remains “locked and loaded” if conditions change.

Does the deployment of another aircraft carrier to the region mean the US-Israel war on Iran is going to resume?

Named after the 26th US president, Theodore Roosevelt, the vessel is a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier.

Commissioned by the US Navy in 1986, the ship carries more than 5,000 personnel and a full air wing of more than 60 aircraft, including F-18s, the twin-engine, supersonic, all-weather multi-role fighter planes.

According to the US Navy, the warship is tasked with “conducting carrier air warfare operations and assisting in the planning, control, coordination and integration of air wing squadrons in support of carrier air warfare”.

Besides combat operations, the carrier also replenishes ships at sea and rescues people, including refugees, at sea.

The USS Theodore Roosevelt has performed combat and humanitarian missions since it was commissioned. During the 1990-91 Gulf War, it was deployed to the Mediterranean and the Red Sea for combat operations. In 2003, it also supported US strikes during the Iraq War.

It was also deployed in the Asia Pacific region from 2020-21 for military exercises with India, Japan, Australia, South Korea and Malaysia.

In October, a US official told Al Jazeera that the USS Theodore Roosevelt had left its San Diego base in September, bound for the Middle East. According to another official, it arrived in the Middle East on November 15 .

But the Pentagon and CENTCOM, which oversees military operations in the region, have not formally confirmed the carrier’s arrival.

What is the state of US deployment in the region?

The arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt in the Middle East brings the total number of US aircraft carrier strike groups operating in the region to three. The USS George Washington and the USS George HW Bush are the other two aircraft carriers currently deployed there.

Last month, a US official told Al Jazeera that the Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group (ARG), carrying more than 2,000 Marines, had also followed the USS Theodore Roosevelt to the Middle East. The Wall Street Journal reported that the strike group and naval deployments could involve an additional 9,000 to 10,000 US soldiers in total, including sailors and Marines assigned to the carrier strike group and other ships. However, the US military is yet to confirm these deployments.

The US has had troops and military assets stationed at bases in the Middle East for decades. Of these, eight are permanent bases, located in Bahrain, Egypt, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. As of mid-2025, there were 40,000 to 50,000 US soldiers stationed in and around the Middle East, including personnel at large, permanent bases and smaller forward sites across the region.

According to open-source intelligence analysts and military flight-tracking data, the US has deployed more than 120 aircraft to the region since early February, before the war on Iran began. That is the biggest surge in US airpower in the Middle East since the Iraq War.

Reported deployments include E-3 Sentry Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) aircraft, F-35 stealth strike fighters and F-22 air superiority jets, alongside F-15s and F-16s. In March, the Pentagon also ordered additional US forces to the Gulf.

The reinforcements consisted of three distinct formations.

The first was the Tripoli ARG, centred around the America-class assault ship USS Tripoli and the 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit (MEU).

The second was the Boxer ARG, built around the Wasp-class assault ship USS Boxer and the 11th MEU, based in southern California in the US.

Together, these two Marine groups have added 4,500 Marines and sailors in the region.

The third was a contingent of about 2,000 soldiers from the 82nd Airborne Division’s Immediate Response Force, based at Fort Bragg, North Carolina. The airborne infantry division is focused on parachute assaults.

In total, nearly 7,000 additional soldiers have already been deployed to the Middle East since the US-Israel war on Iran began.

Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s deputy foreign minister for legal and international affairs, has said the country “will not wait for the US to attack first”.

“The US may be seeking to buy time by abusing diplomacy, in order to prepare the ground for another attack,” he said.

Speaking to state TV in a video released by Iran’s Fars news agency, Gharibabadi warned, “Iran is not Cuba that you can blockade, nor is it Venezuela that you can force to surrender.”

He said US forces “have had no success with either an air blockade or a land blockade” in Iran so far, while the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) is currently producing missiles with “new ranges”.

Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has called for stronger regional energy cooperation, warning US attacks threaten stability across the Middle East.

“Given the increasing impact of US and Israeli aggression on the region’s energy security, strengthening energy cooperation has become an urgent and strategic necessity,” Araghchi said at a meeting of foreign ministers of the Economic Cooperation Organization in Islamabad, Pakistan, on Monday.

“Our region needs not only an independent security framework but also a regional, reliable and sustainable energy mechanism to safeguard energy flows, ensure stable energy supplies, reduce vulnerabilities from external factors, and increase our collective resilience to geopolitical shocks and disruptions,” the IRNA news agency quoted him as saying.

What has the US government said on resuming the war?

The Trump administration has appeared increasingly divided on how to proceed with Iran, since the Republican Party suffered heavy losses in this month’s US midterm elections.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said Washington’s economic pressure campaign against Iran was proving effective, so a resumption of large-scale military operations was likely unnecessary. “The economic pressure on Iran is going to get even worse,” he added.

But Trump has given mixed messages about his plans for the war.

Last week, after a meeting at the White House with Qatar’s prime minister, Trump stated on Truth Social and in a surprise briefing that there was “positive momentum” towards ending the conflict and that a resumption of strikes was “quite unlikely”, declaring the US-Israel war on Iran “effectively over”, militarily.

Still, Trump insisted that the US economic pressure campaign against Iran would stay in place, including a naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz and a more recent task force aimed at cutting off Iran’s trade by land and through the Caspian Sea.

Meanwhile, Iran’s conditions to end the war include an end to the US naval blockade of Iran’s ports, the lifting of economic sanctions, the release of Iranian frozen funds, ending fighting on all fronts and an explicit announcement of an end to the war.

Iranian officials have in recent days underlined that Tehran would not accept the current status quo of “no war, no peace”.

Trump, on his part, has indicated that he is running out of patience with Iran as diplomacy stutters. Last week, the US president said he had told his country’s lead negotiator, Vice President JD Vance, “We don’t need a deal with Iran.”

“Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” he wrote on his Truth Social platform.

So can diplomacy work, or is the region on edge?

Ali Vaez, the International Crisis Group’s Deputy Program Director for the Middle East and North Africa, told Al Jazeera that both sides are caught in a perilous game of chicken, convinced that striking first may be safer than waiting to be struck.

“The danger is that their efforts to deter another war could inadvertently ignite one that neither can win, contain or easily end,” he said.

Diplomatic efforts to stop attacks and reopen the Strait of Hormuz also remain stalled.

In an interview with Al Jazeera last week, Iran’s parliamentary speaker and chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said that Tehran wanted to move beyond a state of “no war, no peace”.

Ghalibaf said Iran had conveyed seven conditions for a deal through a Qatari mediator and was awaiting an official US response. The conditions he outlined included lifting the US naval blockade and sanctions, releasing frozen Iranian funds, ending hostilities on all fronts and formally declaring the war over.

The Trump administration, meanwhile, has tightened sanctions and maintained the blockade on Iranian ports.

“Diplomacy still has a pulse, but it is suffocating under the weight of mutual mistrust and maximalist demands. Unless both sides find a face-saving exit, negotiations risk becoming little more than an intermission between successive rounds of warfare,” Vaez said.

The main issues in the Iran war now are those of sequencing and leverage, according to Rashid al-Mohanadi, vice president at the Center for International Policy Research. He told Al Jazeera that “who does what, when, and how” will determine a potential end of the conflict.

Al-Mohanadi added that the region is clearly against a return to full-scale war, given that regional powers are “leading on the mediation”.

But he warned that the war’s main protagonists appear to have divergent perceptions over their leverage.

“The Iranians perceive they have more leverage. The Americans perceive they have more,” al-Mohanadi said. “When you have a situation like that, reaching a diplomatic end is quite difficult.”

(Al Jazeera)

articles.title: Russell Brand prison message claiming innocence being investigated, No 10 says
articles.summary: Brand's wife read out comments from the comedian on their podcast in which the convicted rapist said he was "not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for".
articles.body:
A message by Russell Brand to his followers in which he claimed innocence for his sexual offences was "clearly appalling" and is being urgently investigated, Downing Street has said.

The comedian is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

His wife Laura read out a message from him on their Sunday Service show on YouTube, in which the convicted rapist claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."

No 10 said it expects action to be taken if Brand is found to have broken prison rules.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the broadcast of a statement from Russell Brand is "completely unacceptable".

In a post on X, Norris wrote: "Prisoners are rightly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims.

"This is being urgently investigated, and I expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules."

In the couple's podcast, released on Sunday, Laura Brand can be seen sitting on a sofa and is holding a Bible with a candle burning in front of her.

Relaying the message from her husband, Laura Brand said the comedian - who is currently being held at HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire - called prison staff "strong", "kind" and "dedicated", and asked people to support his "treasured wife and family".

She said she had been speaking to him and he "is OK and is praying".

Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, and has a large following among believers, including in the US.

Asked about the message, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances.

"Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments."

Speaking earlier, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Sky News: "His crimes are heinous and awful. I think it's revolting, by the way, that he shows no remorse today in his comments."

"No remorse, no sympathy for the victims. Just disgusting comments," he added.

Victims' commissioner for London Andrea Simon said the claims will "certainly retraumatise his victims and other survivors of rape who have to hear it".

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, she added: "The victims during the sentencing hearing highlighted how his denials and ongoing media fame over two decades had added to their pain and trauma.

"The fact survivors are still having to hear this now is really problematic and very concerning that we can't do more to protect them from it."

While freedom of expression allows convicted sex offenders such as Brand to profess their innocence, Simon said terms of service of media platforms should regulate "the way in which they get their message out".

She added that prison rules should also be reviewed to "bar those convicted of sending messages to be broadcast" unless permission is granted by the prison governor.

If Brand is found to have broken prison rules, possible punishments enforceable by prison governors can result in restrictions on social visits or loss of privileges such as access to additional time in the gym or loss of TV.

Governors can also impose proportionate restrictions on communications where justified.

This could include blocking specific phone numbers, increased monitoring of calls or restricting contact with individuals where necessary to protect victims or maintain prison security.

Barristers must stop using rape myths in trials, justice secretary says

Brand moved from Wandsworth to category C prison, his wife confirms on podcast

The Russell Brand I saw in court was not the flamboyant character most people will know

It come as Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy met with senior leaders in media, entertainment, arts and sports organisations as part of her call to end the culture of abuse in industries where there can be large power imbalances.

In the meeting, she asked the leaders what they were doing to create a culture where bullying, harassment and abuse are challenged, how they are empowering whistleblowers to speak out and how their safeguarding systems apply to freelance employees.

The attendees are due to report back to Nandy on the questions she asked them within the coming weeks, the Department for Culture, Media and Sport said.

Over the weekend, Brand was moved from the category B HMP Wandsworth in south London to the category C HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, a prison that mostly houses sex offenders and has tailored programmes for them.

Foreign Office minister Stephen Doughty, told LBC he agreed it was not "a good look" that he'd been moved to a lower security prison.

"I think people want to see him facing the appropriate punishment for what are appalling crimes against women and others and I think the whole episode is shocking," he said.

Meanwhile, there have been calls for a change in the law following Brand's conviction so that sexual relationships between 16 and 17-year-olds and adults would be illegal. The government says a discussion is to take place.

Mia Latter, who has alleged she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16, is among those campaigning for ministers to introduce a staggered age of consent.

She was one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation. Brand denied the allegations at the time. None of the women were complainants in his recent criminal trial.

Latter, who was known under the pseudonym "Alice" in the 2023 investigation, has now waived her right to anonymity.

In an interview with LBC on Monday, Latter said: "We don't want to criminalise anybody under the age of 18 [including] 16, 17-year-olds, 18-year-olds having sex with each other...

"I think healthy relationships are important, and they're important in helping you develop and grow."

But she said there should be an age "threshold" for the partners of 16 and 17 year-olds.

Layla Stone, founder of the campaign group Close the Consent Gap, is urging a change in the law to prevent 16 year-olds from having a sexual relationship with anyone older than 19, and someone aged 17 from having a relationship with anyone older than 20.

She told BBC Breakfast that "predators know exactly what they are doing".

Asked about the issue on BBC Breakfast, the foreign secretary said: "I think the reason why it's right to have this debate is we've seen some of the very, very brave victims of Russell Brand come forward and say 'we think this needs looking at'".

Shadow education secretary Laura Trott said she is glad there is a conversation around staggering the age of consent but warned that it had "been quite complicated to actually implement" in some US states where it is used.

Trott said a suggestion that the age of consent should be raised to 18 is also a "conversation we need to have" but "probably isn't practical".

Anna Edmundson, director of policy & social change at the NSPCC charity, said: "We urgently need a review of what is and isn't working to ensure 16 and 17-year-olds are fully protected in law from this predatory behaviour.

"However, closing these gaps will only be part of the solution. We must question why adults have been able to exploit teenagers in plain sight for so long, and look at what further action is needed to help people recognise the signs of exploitation."

Any change in the law would only affect England and Wales as Scotland and Northern Ireland have separate legislative powers in relation to the age of consent, which is also currently set at 16 in both nations.

The Scottish Government said it had "no current plans" to change the age of consent, following the calls by campaigners, but any proposals would be considered.

The foreign secretary also apologised for having appeared on Russell Brand's online show in 2015, when he was Labour leader.

Miliband told Today if he'd known about the allegations then, he would not have done spoken to him, adding: "I deeply regret doing that interview and all my sympathies are with those victims."

articles.title: Parnell Square: Man sentenced for attempted murder of three children
articles.summary: Riad Bouchaker was sentenced after the attempted murder of three children in November 2023.
articles.body:
A 52-year-old man has been sentenced to life in prison for the attempted murder of three children outside a primary school in Dublin's Parnell Square in November 2023.

On Monday, Judge Tony Hunt imposed the overall sentence of life imprisonment in Dublin's Central Criminal Court.

Rioting across many parts of Dublin following the attack led to the deployment of the most riot police in Irish history.

Bouchaker was originally from Algeria but had lived in Ireland for 25 years prior to the attack, and he had Irish citizenship.

He was assisted by an Arabic interpreter and a speech-and-language expert during the trial, who were present in court for the sentencing.

The attack took place outside Gaelscoil Choláiste Mhuire in Parnell Square, shortly after 13:40 local time on 23 November.

A group of 13 children, aged five and six, were lined up on Parnell Square waiting to go to their afterschool provision. Childcare worker Leanne Flynn was helping a little boy zip up his jacket when Bouchaker pulled his knife on the children.

A five-year-old girl was left with a lifelong brain injury after being stabbed in the heart.

Now eight, she is non-verbal and can only communicate by blinking, uses a wheelchair and has to be fed through a tube in her stomach as she cannot swallow safely by herself.

The judge said the child will never live independently and that her life, and the lives of her family, had been permanently altered.

He also noted that Flynn suffered life-threatening injuries, including a collapsed lung and the loss of a spleen, as well as profound psychological consequences and her services not being available to children.

The judge said she had acted fearlessly to protect the children and hoped she could return to work in the future, but said the possibility of such remains an unanswered question.

Speaking outside court Garda (Irish police) Det Supt Colm Murphy acknowledged the actions of those "who immediately reacted the to the situation as it unfolded, in particular to Leanne Flynn – her actions on the day saved lives".

Murphy, who was the senior investigating officer in charge added: "To those who intervened and stopped the attack again, their actions saved lives".

He also gave praise to medical personnel on the ground and hospital staff, saying that they too "saved lives".

Murphy also acknowledged the principal of Gaelscoil Choláiste Mhuire, "for the way he and the staff at the school reacted on the day", and also to the parents who had to endure such a traumatic incident".

Judge Hunt said this was an unprecedented, highly unusual case involving a sudden, ferocious, sustained attack on young children and their childcare worker.

He said he had to mark the exceptional gravity of the offending against very young children and their carer, with a lethal weapon leading to consequences of the utmost gravity.

He said the circumstances were uniquely horrific and marked a profound assault on the most fundamental values protected by the criminal law.

The judge said the children happened to be selected because they were there and he was not yet sure what inference could be drawn from how Bouchaker found himself at their collection point.

At an earlier hearing, the court heard he received brain surgery in 2021 and a portion of his skull was removed, leaving a part of his brain vulnerable.

He suffered a head injury when members of the public intervened during the Parnell Square attack, after which he received hospital treatment for a month.

His defence team, which the judge ordered cannot be named due to safety concerns, said Bouchaker's cognitive function, memory, concentration, communication and decision-making were affected as a result of the impairment.

The most riot police in Irish state history were deployed to deal with the unrest.

Within hours of the attack, rioters destroyed 11 police vehicles, while 13 shops were badly damaged and more were looted during clashes with riot police.

Three buses and a tram were also destroyed and several police officers were injured during three hours of sustained violence.

Ireland's police chief at the time, Drew Harris blamed the rioting on a "lunatic, hooligan faction driven by a far-right ideology".

images.caption: In July Riad Bouchaker was found guilty of the eight charges he faced

articles.title: Who is Ahmad Tibi, the Arab MP elected deputy speaker of Israel’s Knesset?
articles.summary: A Palestinian citizen of Israel, Tibi was an aide to Yasser Arafat and has been a legislator for 27 years.
articles.body:
Ahmad Tibi, chairman of the Arab Movement for Renewal (Ta’al) party, has been elected deputy speaker of the Israeli Knesset. The appointment marks a significant milestone for the seasoned lawmaker who has long represented Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Speaking to Al Jazeera following his election, Tibi framed the moment as a victory against far-right parties that have led or been part of Israel’s government in recent years.

“This is a rightful achievement for the Joint List, which secured 11 seats,” he said, referring to an alliance of Arab-majority parties.

“Likud and Ben-Gvir attempted to prevent my election, but they failed despite their reckless incitement,” Tibi added, referring to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s party and far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.

Born in the city of Taibe on December 19, 1958, to a family displaced from Jaffa during the 1948 Nakba, Tibi initially pursued medicine, graduating with top honours from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in 1983. However, his political activism soon overshadowed his medical career.

In 1984, Tibi met Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) leader Yasser Arafat in Tunis, Tunisia, defying Israeli laws that classified it as a “terrorist organisation” at the time.

Although interrogated by Israeli police upon his return, he was never formally charged. Tibi later served as a political adviser to Arafat between 1993 and 1999. He acted as the Palestinian delegation’s spokesperson at the Wye River summit in Maryland, United States, in 1998.

Benjamin Netanyahu, the longest-serving Israeli prime minister, was then in his first stint in power. At the summit, Israel agreed to withdraw its forces from parts of the occupied West Bank, while the Palestinian Authority (PA) agreed to a further crackdown on armed factions of the Palestinian resistance movement. Like other Israel-Palestine accords, the Wye River Memorandum was soon abandoned by Israel.

Tibi founded Ta’al in 1996 and was first elected to the Knesset in 1999. Identifying himself as an “Arab Palestinian with Israeli citizenship”, he advocates for a two-state solution and the right of return for Palestinian refugees. He consistently challenges Israel’s definition as a “Jewish state”, describing it instead as an “apartheid state” and advocating for a “state for all its citizens”.

His outspoken positions and on-the-ground activism have repeatedly made him a target of the Israeli government and violent far-right activists.

During the second Intifada in September 2000, his right hand was broken while confronting Ariel Sharon, who would become prime minister the following year, during his provocative storming of the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound.

In 2002, Israel stripped Tibi of his parliamentary immunity after he entered the Jenin refugee camp during a military offensive and confronted soldiers.

Tibi is also renowned for his dramatic parliamentary protests. In 2016, he famously raised the Islamic call to prayer inside the Knesset chamber to protest against a proposed Israeli bill aiming to ban loudspeakers in Jerusalem and the occupied Palestinian territory.

articles.title: Microsoft reveals the cause of its catastrophic Outlook outage — incident set off by a ‘cascading failure’ of servers as crash leads to chlorine gas poisoning of 15 hotel guests
articles.summary: The Microsoft 365 crash led to 15 hotel guests suffering chlorine gas poisoning, with Microsoft revealing the outage’s cause.
articles.body:
When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission.

The Microsoft 365 outage led to a key safety system failing in Germany

This caused the chlorine gas poisoning of 15 hotel guests

Microsoft has since revealed exactly what caused the outage

If you were affected by last week's global Microsoft 365 outage , chances are you had trouble accessing your email. You probably didn't expect to be poisoned as a result, yet that's exactly what happened to over a dozen unfortunate hotel guests in Germany — but Microsoft has reported that the blackout wasn't caused by a cyberattack.

According to a news report from German outlet WDR (via Notebookcheck ), 15 guests at a hotel for the Phantasialand theme park were injured when the park's swimming pool received excessive levels of chlorine. This was caused by a malfunction in the chlorine monitoring system, but because alerts are sent to park staff over email — and because those email systems were down due to the Microsoft 365 outage — no one knew about the problem until guests started getting sick.

According to a Facebook post made by the fire department that responded to the incident, 40 first responders were dispatched and 15 guests were triaged after the chlorine gas leak. WDR reported that the affected people suffered from respiratory irritation, with four needing to be taken to hospital.

The episode illustrates the serious — and often unexpected — consequences that can arise when something as central to a business's operations as an email system goes down. When it's responsible for important safety procedures, the results can be potentially life-threatening.

Since the outage, Microsoft has said that full service has been resumed. It has since published a post-incident report , which is available in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center portal. The full write up has also been relayed on Reddit .

In the report, Microsoft revealed that the outage was caused by three principal factors: a "latent defect" from July that overwhelmed Windows servers; a Microsoft Teams failure that increased the load on a system shared with Microsoft Exchange ; and the fact that 14% of server capacity for the networking system was out of service at the time.

Taken individually, these factors were not enough to cause the global failure. But when the increased load and the lower server capacity combined, they triggered the latent defect. Server requests then piled up until the servers stopped responding — which happened to occur during the peak traffic window for the United States.

As a mitigation effort, traffic was automatically redirected towards healthy endpoints. However, this process made those endpoints more likely to themselves encounter the latent defect. "This caused a cascading failure from server to server as the same amount of load was spread across fewer servers," Microsoft wrote. At its worst point, the outage had caused 80% of available servers to become unresponsive.

Due to a separate issue, Microsoft's bulwarks against such a cascading failure did not function properly. Recovery took longer than expected because restored servers were immediately overwhelmed by pent up traffic, making them fail once again. And because the latent defect dated back to July, simply rolling back to a recent version was not enough.

To fix the outage once and for all, Microsoft had to return its code path to that of a previously good state, then take servers offline in batches, roll out the patch across its infrastructure, then restart its systems. Eventually, service was restored.

The post-incident report is a sobering reminder of what can happen when several seemingly independent issues can converge all at once, and of the consequences that are possible when that happens on such a large scale. And as the chlorine incident in Germany demonstrates, these failures often go beyond mere technical disruption and touch on people's health and wellbeing.

articles.title: Which cricket teams can qualify for the LA 2028 Olympics and how?
articles.summary: Six men’s and six women’s teams will compete for the medals in T20 format as cricket returns to the Olympics in 2028.
articles.body:
Cricket has moved one step closer to its Olympic comeback with the unveiling of a qualification process in advance of the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics, where the sport will feature in its shortest format.

Eight men’s and women’s teams will have one last chance to feature in the Twenty20 competition at the LA Games, according to the plan announced by the International Cricket Council (ICC) on Sunday.

The world’s second-most popular sport has billions of followers around the world, particularly in South Asia, which has secured five of the 10 men’s T20 world championships.

Despite its global popularity, cricket has not featured at the Olympics since 1900, when Great Britain defeated France in the only match played.

The sport’s Olympic return was overwhelmingly approved in October 2023 in what was described as a “win-win situation”.

“The Olympic Games will give cricket a global stage and the opportunity to grow beyond the traditional cricket countries and regions,” then president of the International Olympic Committee, Thomas Bach, said after the IOC announced its decision.

Here’s everything to know about the Olympic qualifiers:

Six men’s and six women’s teams will feature at the Olympics.

Four teams automatically qualify based on ICC rankings in the Asia, Europe, Oceania and Africa regions.

One spot goes to the host nation (USA), subject to the side being ranked 15th or better in the Twenty20 International (T20I) standings during the qualification period.

The sixth and final place goes to the team winning its qualifier.

When and where are the Olympic cricket qualifiers?

The men’s qualifiers will take place from February 5 to 13, 2028, in Bangladesh, followed by the women’s qualifiers from February 26 to March 5 in the United States.

Which teams have qualified for the Olympics?

Four women’s teams — India, Great Britain (through England), Australia and South Africa — have already qualified after finishing as the top-ranked sides in Asia, Europe, Oceania and Africa, respectively, in the women’s T20 World Cup this year.

No men’s teams have qualified yet. The highest-ranked sides from the four regions as of December 31, 2026, when the qualification period ends, will secure spots.

Both the men’s and women’s tournaments will feature a total of eight teams divided into groups of four. Each team will play the other teams in their group once.

The group winners will progress to the final, with an Olympic berth at stake.

Are any teams ineligible to compete at the Olympics?

Yes, the West Indies will not be able to compete at the Olympics because the team consists of multiple Caribbean nations, which are represented by their respective national Olympic committees (NOCs), not a unified one.

If the West Indies rank among the eight highest sides yet to qualify, a dedicated Caribbean tournament will be organised to determine which nation will represent the region at the qualifiers.

Where and when will cricket be held at LA28?

Cricket will be played at the $21m, 15,000-seat Knight Riders Cricket Ground in Pomona, about 31 miles (50km) east of downtown Los Angeles.

The women’s tournament will be held from July 12 to 20, followed by the men’s tournament from July 22 to 29.

The purpose-built venue hosted its first competitive match in July when the Los Angeles Knight Riders took on Washington Freedom in Major League Cricket.

Which sports are making their Olympic debut at LA 2028?

Squash, lacrosse and flag football will feature at the games for the first time.

Will cricket be a permanent feature of the Olympics?

Cricket is not yet confirmed for the 2032 Games in Brisbane, Australia, but the ICC is hopeful the sport will make the cut.

articles.title: Mamdani guts elite NYPD tactical unit, backs 'civilian-led approach' to responding to protests
articles.summary: Zohran Mamdani disbands the NYPD Strategic Response Group and unveils a civilian-led dialogue team to handle New York City protest response.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced the disbanding of the NYPD's Strategic Response Group (SRG) on Monday, saying the city will now pursue a "civilian-led approach" to responding to protests. Mamdani made the announcement alongside Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch, stating that the SRG's counterterrorism functions will be folded into an existing command, while a brand-new organization will now lead protest response, the Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division (CDDD). The CDDD, which will lie within the Mayor's Office of Community Safety, will work to "improve the NYPD's protest response" via a specialized "dialogue team," known as the First Amendment Support Team (FAST), they said. "The CDDD will not have weapons or arrest powers. FAST will consist of 30 uniformed officers trained in communication and de-escalation. The NYPD will also establish a new Patrol Support Division (PSD), a unit within the NYPD’s Patrol Services Bureau, with vetted officers who will spend most of their time on patrol-related duties and receive specialized crowd management training to support responses to demonstrations," the mayor's office said in a statement. NYC MAYOR ZOHRAN MAMDANI SAYS HE WON'T FIRE NYPD COMMISSIONER JESSICA TISCH DESPITE SOCIALIST PRESSURE "During our campaign, I promised New Yorkers that we would disband the Strategic Response Group and separate counterterrorism from protest response, and today we are delivering on that promise," Mamdani said in a statement. MINNEAPOLIS PROGRESSIVES TURN ON GEORGE FLOYD-ERA PUBLIC SAFETY OVERHAUL, PUSH TO DISMANTLE OFFICE "New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat. We are establishing a new, civilian-led approach that prioritizes dialogue, engagement and de-escalation," he added. The reforms also impose new restrictions on the tools police are allowed to use when responding to protests, including codified bans on kettling, long guns and tear gas. Pepper spray will also not be used as a crowd management tool, and "long-range acoustic devices" will be limited to 90 decibels. MAMDANI, NYPD GIVE SECURITY UPDATE AHEAD OF JEWISH HIGH HOLY DAYS, 9/11 25TH ANNIVERSARY Under the previous structure, the NYPD said the SRG responded to citywide mobilizations, civil disorders and major events and was a "critical asset" during parades, protests and the papal visit. SRG personnel were "also deployed to areas requiring an increased police presence due to increased crime or other conditions" and "mobilizes for shootings, bank robberies, missing persons, demonstrations, or other significant incidents," according to the department. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Tisch noted at a March budget hearing that the SRG did not typically deal with peaceful protests, but was deployed for protests that involved criminal activity. She also noted that in 2025, the NYPD facilitated 4,255 protests and the SRG was available at 245 of them, or roughly 6%.

articles.title: Design for Northampton M1 tourism sign is approved
articles.summary: A campaign group celebrates approval from National Highways for its design.
articles.body:
The design for a brown sign which would promote tourism in Northamptonshire has been approved, a campaign group has said.

The On The Map group, made up of business people from the county, submitted the 85-page application in February.

It would be situated on the M1 northbound at junction 15 and businessman John Henderson said the approval from National Highways was "fantastic" news.

The group will need to raise money for the sign's production and installation.

"There's quite a bit of work to do to make sure it's in the right place," said Henderson.

The sign will read "historic Northamptonshire - follow A45" and Henderson hopes it will attract some of the estimated 140,000 drivers who pass the junction every day.

The design features symbols to represent Northampton Museum and Art Gallery, All Saints' Church, the historical 78 Derngate house and the town's tourism information office.

The two crossed swords denote Delapre Abbey, which was a battlefield in the 15th Century.

"You have to direct people to particular destinations and attractions," said Henderson.

"We're trying to promote the cultural quarter to get people into that area of the town and obviously the tourist information centre provides more information going forward.

"What we don't want is people driving up and down the A45, [with] hazard warning lights, not knowing where they're going."

The group wants to fundraise £80,000 to complete the project and it is holding an event at the Mercure Hotel in Northampton on 11 March.

articles.title: Barristers must stop using rape myths in trials, justice secretary says
articles.summary: Russell Brand's barrister has been accused of peddling rape myths while defending the comedian.
articles.body:
The justice secretary has called for new rules to prevent barristers from using rape myths to defend their clients in the wake of the Russell Brand trial.

As first reported by the Times , in a letter to the Bar Standards Board (BSB), Alex Norris said it was "unacceptable" to "perpetuate myths" about victims in court and disciplinary action could be taken against those who do so.

In his closing speech, Brand's defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, questioned why his client's accusers had not fought back.

The BSB said it had set up an expert group this year to advise on "strengthening standards for barristers", while the Bar Council said defendants had a "right to have evidence tested in court".

Russell Brand prison message denying rape 'appalling' and being investigated, No 10 says

Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Winter said to the court "not one of them [Brand's accusers] resisted or screamed or even tried to leave".

Winter also asked the jury if they could be sure that out of the "many, many women" Brand had had sex with over a decade, "he raped just three of them".

Norris wrote in his letter to the BSB: "[The board] must send a strong signal to the profession on the harm arising from rape myths, and that the perpetuation of such myths within a court room is unacceptable, just as they are unacceptable in our society at large."

The charity Rape Crisis says it is "really common for people who experience rape, sexual assault, sexual abuse or other types of sexual violence to find they can't move or speak".

The judge presiding over Brand's case was praised by the Criminal Bar Association and campaign groups for comments he made during his sentencing remarks to dispel rape myths.

Mr Justice Bennathan told Southwark Crown Court: "Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts when sexual predators like you, Russell Brand, act without their consent."

A spokesperson for the BSB said such cases "must be decided on the basis of the evidence and not prejudice", adding: "Any other approach may discourage others from coming forward and adversely affect public confidence in the criminal justice system more widely."

Kirsty Brimelow KC, chair of the Bar Council of England and Wales which is part of the group examining the need for further training, said it was important for the BSB to remain "independent of the government".

She told BBC Radio 4's Woman's Hour that a "regulatory gap" had not been made clear to her and there were already powers to discipline barristers if breaches of the code of conduct happen.

She said training for "vulnerable witnesses" was already undertaken but it could be "problematic" if it was made mandatory.

Brimelow said there were currently a lack of barristers defending cases of rape and sexual assault and the possibility of further compulsory training could see more pushed out.

"What I wouldn't like to see is publicity around one case to take a life of its own rather than looking at what we already do," she told the BBC.

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Justice said the justice secretary was "determined to make protections for victims as strong as possible".

"Rape myths have absolutely no place in our courts, giving evidence in cases of this nature is a brave act and can be traumatic for victims: they must never feel as though they are the ones on trial," the spokesperson said.

"Independent judges are already able to, and do, give directions to counter rape myths but we always want to keep looking at ways we can improve how the entire justice system treats victims of sexual violence."

In an interview with the BBC earlier this month, Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said some of the comments made at the trial he had seen reported were "getting very close to victim blaming".

He also backed calls for a law change that would require judges to direct juries on rape myths and misconceptions in every rape trial.

"It shouldn't be possible for inaccurate statements to be made to a jury to suggest that because a rape victim didn't behave in one way that somehow undermines their case," Sir Mark said.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the government needs to make sure victims of rape cases do not feel like they are on trial .

articles.title: Miliband: I won't resign if government approves Rosebank oil field
articles.summary: Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is to make a decision on Britain's largest untapped oil field.
articles.body:
Ed Miliband said he will "definitely not" resign if the government approves the Rosebank oil field, despite previously calling the scheme "climate vandalism".

The foreign secretary told the BBC he would "obey collective responsibility", which requires ministers to publicly support decisions made by the government even if they disagree with them.

A decision on the future of the oil field off Shetland will be taken by Miatta Fahnbulleh, who succeeded Miliband as energy secretary in July.

Some Labour MPs oppose the project, while the Conservatives argue there is a need to "get Britain drilling". Miliband publicly raised his concerns about Rosebank while Labour was in opposition.

Appearing on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Miliband was reminded that in 2023 he said the project would be a "colossal waste of taxpayer money and climate vandalism" .

Asked if it could be assumed he would resign if his successor decided to develop Rosebank, Miliband replied: "No, definitely not because I obey collective responsibility.

"Miatta Fahnbulleh will make the decision on this. As you know, it's what they call a quasi-judicial decision so she looks at all the evidence and then reaches a conclusion."

Miliband said he would not "second guess her decision" on Rosebank.

He added he supported the energy secretary recently giving the green light to the Jackdaw gas field after years of uncertainty and a court case.

Pressed further about his previous remarks on Rosebank, Miliband said: "I'm a member of the government and I will abide by collective responsibility on this."

He went on to say there are "direct and very bad impacts at home" for the cost of living linked to Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the Iran conflict.

Miliband added: "What does that teach us? That we can't get economic and energy security from fossil fuels, we've got to keep on with this transition to wind power, solar power, nuclear power; homegrown clean energy we can control."

Catherine Fookes is among a group of Labour MPs, reported to number at least 75, who have signed a letter opposing Rosebank.

The MP for Monmouthshire told Today: "We need to really look at what we're doing and ensure we don't exacerbate our climate challenges and make climate change worse.

"And that's exactly what drilling in the North Sea would do."

Steve Yemm, Labour MP for Mansfield, offered his support to Rosebank and said it would be a "test of whether, as a country, we can support investment and skilled work in the North Sea whilst meeting our climate obligations".

One Labour MP, who is pro Rosebank, said they were increasingly confident the decision would go their way, but added the "gloves will now come off" after Fookes's intervention.

They said people on both sides of the argument had been attempting to avoid so-called "red on red" clashes but predicted Labour MPs would now start to disagree more forcefully in public about the issue.

The same MP accused Miliband of "running two departments" and said the current group of energy ministers were "all his people" and "all coming from the same place".

They said they were becoming increasingly frustrated with Labour MPs who opposed Rosebank and added "Trump is right, we do need to open the North Sea".

Some people in Parliament believe that a decision on the oil field could be made as soon as the end of this month.

Rosebank is Britain's largest untapped oil field and would also produce some gas. It is about 80 miles (128km) north-west of Shetland.

In 2023, the then Conservative UK government granted a licence for Rosebank and a legal challenge followed.

The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that the government had made the approval unlawfully, leaving the current Labour government to make a new decision on whether to give the go-ahead.

If approved, Rosebank is expected to fill up to 500m barrels of oil over its 25-year lifetime.

But prices are determined by international markets, which means there is no guarantee that increased supply would result in cheaper energy bills in the UK.

Environmental campaigners believe approval of Rosebank would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and would have no meaningful impact on the UK's energy security or bills.

They have also argued that Rosebank would be even more damaging for the environment than Jackdaw, as it would produce far more planet-warming greenhouse gases.

The UK is committed to reaching net zero by 2050 - meaning the UK must cut carbon emissions until it removes as much as it produces - and wants to limit global warming to no more than 1.5C above the pre-industrial period.

On Monday, it was announced that gas has begun flowing from the Jackdaw gas field .

Conservative shadow energy secretary Andrew Bowie said: "One gas field does not make an energy strategy.

"Labour cannot claim to back the North Sea while continuing to block new licences, undermine investor confidence, and hammer the industry with a punishing windfall tax."

Bowie added "it is clear that Labour cannot be trusted to deliver the energy security we need" with some of the party's MPs "seemingly poised to rebel" over the approval of Rosebank.

articles.title: 'Fight on' call after Lincolnshire solar farm challenge fails
articles.summary: A campaigner says Lincolnshire County Council should continue its opposition to new projects.
articles.body:
An anti-solar farm campaigner says he would be "gutted" if local authorities "rolled over" and stopped opposing more farms being built.

Lincolnshire County Council's legal challenge to Springwell Solar Farm near Sleaford, the biggest in the country, was thrown out by the High Court last week .

Council leader Sean Matthews said the decision "may have set a precedent for this kind of challenge", raising questions over the future of a legal challenge to Beacon Fen Energy Park at nearby Heckington.

But campaigner Marc Williams said the council should "stand up for us" and continue to fight planned future developments.

Matthews said the failed Springwell challenge had been worth doing, but said he looked "at the money that we spend very, very carefully".

"I've got to be realistic and I've got to take a pragmatic view, but we'll sit down as councillors and officers and come to a decision on Beacon Fen shortly," he said.

Earlier this year, the government said giving its backing to the Springwell scheme was a reflection of "growing government investment in solar power to deliver clean energy and help lower bills".

Ed Miliband, who was energy secretary at the time, said: "Record-breaking solar growth means greater energy security, lower exposure to volatile fossil fuel markets which we can't control."

Williams, one of the leaders of the Springwell Solar Action group, said he "was disgusted by the overall decision, but not surprised".

The group had opposed the plans over their "sheer size" and the use of prime agricultural land.

He said he understood the council's "nervousness" over continuing to spend money on a further legal challenge.

"In the grand scheme of things, we're talking about pennies per resident in Lincolnshire, but in a time of economic issues, every penny does count," he said.

"But I also think that for the people of Lincolnshire, we expect our local councils to stand up for us, and they should fight it.

"I'd be gutted if they rolled over, but I do understand their concern."

The Beacon Fen project will be capable of powering up to 130,000 homes while Springwell Solar Farm will be able to power 180,000.

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said the climate crisis was the biggest threat to agriculture and nature.

A spokesperson said: "Solar is one of the cheapest and quickest forms of energy to build, helping get bills down for good."

articles.title: Lindsay Clancy retrial scheduled for March over the strangulation deaths of her three children
articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy’s retrial for the killings of her three young children in 2023 has been set for March, a Massachusetts judge said Monday.
articles.body: Lindsay Clancy’s retrial for the killings of her three young children in 2023 has been set for March, a Massachusetts judge said Monday. Clancy and her team appeared in court for a status hearing that set the date for her retrial. Judge William Sullivan last week did not rule in favor of the defense’s motion to dismiss all charges against Clancy, paving the way for a retrial. The retrial will start March 29, giving both sides four months to prepare. The final pretrial hearing will be March 18. Clancy’s first trial ended in a mistrial in September after jurors said a holdout prevented the nine women and three men from reaching a unanimous decision. In the weeks following the mistrial, defense attorney Kevin Reddington filed a motion to dismiss the three murder charges. Clancy is accused of strangling her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months old — with exercise bands on the night of Jan. 24, 2023, before throwing herself out of her bedroom window in a suicide attempt that left her paralyzed and in a wheelchair. She has been charged with three counts of first-degree murder. Her defense has argued that she was in the throes of postpartum psychosis when she carried out the killings and therefore was unaware of her actions at the time. The prosecution, however, argued that she planned the killings ahead of time and was not actually in psychosis when she murdered the children. It remains unclear whether the arguments on both sides will remain the same in the next trial. Reddington, after court Monday, said he was surprised that the prosecution intends to pursue the first-degree murder charges against Clancy for a second time. “I mean, they have an indictment, they have a right to go forward on it,” Reddington said. “I’m a little disappointed with the way it shook out today, but they have a right to do that.” After Sullivan ruled against the motion to dismiss Clancy’s charges, the prosecution had to decide whether to move ahead with a new trial. Prosecutors could also have reduced the charges, moved to a bench trial, offered a plea deal, or dropped the charges altogether. Martin Weinberg, an attorney on Clancy’s defense team, argued for the motion to dismiss charges, saying in court Nov. 2 that the prosecution had to meet the manifest necessity standard to warrant a mistrial and, in turn, a retrial. He argued that the court should have questioned the holdout juror when he refused to participate in negotiations, and if his reasons were personal, the court could have discharged him, allowing deliberations to continue with another juror. That did not happen, he said. The jury foreperson returned three deadlock notes before Sullivan declared a mistrial, but Sullivan did not voir dire the juror — meaning question the juror to determine whether they could be fair and impartial — and declared a mistrial before replacing him with an alternate. Reddington then attempted a last-minute emergency stay, but Supreme Judicial Court Associate Justice Dalila Argaez Wendlandt later denied it. On Nov. 2, the prosecution argued that the court must determine whether manifest necessity was met based on what happened in court and what the court knew at the time of the mistrial — not what happened afterward or what the media revealed. It also asked the judge to deny the motion Oct. 29. Following the mistrial, several other jurors spoke out, including the jury foreperson, and described the holdout as someone who refused to participate in discussions. They also said he did not apply the reasonable doubt standard when wanting to convict Clancy of first-degree murder. The holdout juror, Michael Desronvil, has since said he has felt harassed since the end of the trial and insisted in an interview that he “didn’t have any doubts.” On Nov. 9, Sullivan also ruled on two other motions discussed in court the week prior. Sullivan denied Clancy’s motion to question the holdout juror in the trial and examine court records related to his service. The prosecution was also handed a loss on one of its motions in court last week — Sullivan rejected its bid to prevent lawyers from freely discussing the case with the media. Clancy’s initial trial captivated the nation, prompting online sleuths to probe the unique case — and reach their own conclusions. For the duration of the trial, a faction of posters insisted that Clancy couldn’t have carried out the killings, and that her then-husband, Patrick Clancy, did instead, framing her. Reddington on Monday said he wouldn’t be surprised if the second trial gets the same national attention. “I don’t know what the temperature would be as far as media, and I think it would probably be pretty intense,” he said, adding that Clancy’s case covers a lot of issues that “a lot of people are concerned with,” such as mental health and women’s health. In an interview days after the mistrial, Reddington said Clancy rejects the conspiracy theories about Patrick Clancy. He also said Clancy, at the time, “was not very good” and remained “suicidal.” On Monday, he reiterated that Clancy and her family are “not good” but that her family is “very supportive.” If you or someone you know is in crisis, call 988 to reach the National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. You can also call the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 800-273-8255, text HOME to 741741 or visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources for additional resources.

articles.title: Iraq deploys army to stronghold of Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah
articles.summary: US pressure on Iraq to curb Tehran’s influence leaves potential for direct confrontation with Iran-linked armed group.
articles.body:
Iraq has ordered its armed forces to move into a stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah group, amid an investigation into suspected oil smuggling.

Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has ordered the military to enter the town of Jurf al-Nasr, government spokesman Haidar al-Aboudi said on Monday, according to the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA). The Iraqi leader has also set a deadline for the armed faction, which has been implicated in the oil probe, to leave the area.

The order comes amid pressure on Baghdad from the United States and some of its Gulf-state allies to counter Tehran’s influence in Iraq.

Al-Aboudi told local media the “deadline is not far off”. A senior Iraqi official told Al Jazeera Arabic that Kataib Hezbollah has until Friday to leave Jurf al-Nasr, which sits south of Baghdad in the centre of the country and was previously known as Jurf al-Sakhar.

Al-Zaidi told military and security commanders to deploy additional forces around the town and to prepare for government troops to enter. The order would potentially bring the government and its troops into direct confrontation with the armed group.

Security agencies have also been instructed to prevent tankers carrying oil or petroleum products from leaving the area.

Iraq recently launched a sweeping anticorruption crackdown centred on the town, which allegedly harbours illicit oil refineries.

Kataib Hezbollah, one of dozens of heavily armed pro-Iranian groups that have semi-official status in Iraq, denied the allegations on Sunday, saying that an inspection found no interference with pipelines.

“We are therefore being subjected to the greatest campaign of blackmail aimed at forcing us to relinquish the weapons of dignity that have upheld sovereignty and protected the rights of Iraqis at multiple stages,” the group said in a statement.

The campaign to stamp out the oil smuggling trade has seen the dismissal and judicial referral of nine senior officials accused of corruption. It has also led to the sacking of senior government officials and security directors.

Al-Aboudi said an investigative committee, following an intelligence agency report, had “detected clear tampering with pipelines passing through the area, as well as attempts to bury and conceal traces of that tampering”.

Sources told the Reuters news agency that the smuggling , carried out with accomplices among some security and oil officials, has robbed the government of hundreds of millions of dollars since 2021.

While officially framed as an initiative to protect public funds, analysts believe the oil probe is a calculated strategy to sever the financial arteries of armed factions that refuse to integrate into Iraq’s state apparatus.

Iranian-backed armed groups, including Kataib Hezbollah, have resisted repeated calls by both al-Zaidi and ‌‌‌‌his ally, US President Donald Trump, to disarm.

They have struck US troops and targets in Saudi Arabia and the UAE in solidarity with Tehran since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran in February.

articles.title: 'No money left': French far-right leader Le Pen vows to cut off Ukraine aid if elected president
articles.summary: The French far-right has separated itself from providing financial assistance to Ukraine, with far-right leader Marine Le Pen promising to stop aid within
articles.body: The French far-right has separated itself from providing financial assistance to Ukraine, with far-right leader Marine Le Pen promising to stop aid within six months of taking office.Le Pen, who has declined Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy's invitation to visit Kyiv, has offered to meet him in Brussels instead. She said the Belgian capital would be a more appropriate venue because the question of funding Ukraine had become a major point of debate across Europe.The National Rally (RN) leader is expected to discuss her position with Ukraine's ambassador to France on Monday. Her pledge would cover both direct French assistance and contributions to European Union funding arrangements, according to Renaud Labaye, her deputy campaign director.“If we win, 2028 will see the end of financial aid, including through the European Union,” Labaye told Le Monde.France's withdrawal could hit Ukraine's war effortA French retreat would carry significant consequences for Kyiv. France has provided around 27 billion euros in bilateral and European assistance to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, according to calculations by the Kiel Institute for the World Economy. It is the second-largest European contributor after Germany.Paris accounts for about 18% of European funding plans for Ukraine. Le Pen's proposal would therefore go beyond stopping direct aid and could weaken the wider European effort to support the country.The RN has suggested it could continue some forms of non-financial assistance, including military training, while allowing weapons to be supplied on a commercial basis.Le Pen has justified her position by pointing to France's strained public finances and the cost-of-living pressures facing its citizens. Labaye said the country no longer had the financial capacity to sustain its current level of support.Macron accuses opponents of pushing Ukraine towards an unjust peaceFrench president Emmanuel Macron criticised the proposal on Saturday without naming Le Pen directly. He argued that restricting resources for Ukraine would ultimately force the country into an unjust settlement and leave both Ukraine and Europe more vulnerable.“Those who want to ration resources for Ukraine ultimately want to force it into an unjust peace,” Macron wrote on social media.Le Pen hit back, blaming Macron's economic record for France's financial difficulties. “If the president had not ruined our country over the past 10 years, there would still be room to continue financial aid to Ukraine,” she told Agence France-Presse.Her position could also put Paris at odds with Berlin. German chancellor Friedrich Merz had warned on November 9 that European funds could be withheld from countries that refused to support Ukraine. Le Pen described the warning as “blackmail” and accused Merz of disregarding democracy and national sovereignty.Le Pen faces divisions within her own party over RussiaThe Ukraine question has exposed differences within the RN, where some figures remain sympathetic to Moscow while others have sought to distance the party from its earlier pro-Russian positions.Le Pen has long faced criticism over her past closeness to Russian president Vladimir Putin and her recognition of Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014. After Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, she adopted a more critical tone. In September, she described Russia as a threat to France and condemned what she called Russian intelligence operations aimed at undermining support for Ukraine.However, some of her close advisers continue to express views more favourable to Moscow.European Parliament member Thierry Mariani, said it was right that Le Pen had declined to visit Ukraine, arguing that the French president should not be “at Zelenskyy's service”.Political scientist Frédéric Charillon told Le Monde that Le Pen was balancing the views of a pro-Russian section of her electorate against the need to attract more moderate conservative voters. Her focus on the financial cost of supporting Ukraine, he said, offered a way to maintain distance from Moscow without appearing openly aligned with it.Kyiv watches the French election cautiouslyZelenskyy has sought to play down the prospect of a change in France's political direction. Asked about Le Pen, he said Ukraine would work with whoever French voters elected, while praising Macron's support for a Europe in which Ukraine had a place.He also pointed out that the European Union had 27 member states, not just France, suggesting that support for Kyiv would not depend on a single government.Ukrainian lawmakers have nevertheless acknowledged concerns about the possibility of a Le Pen presidency. Yelyzaveta Yasko, a member of Zelenskyy's party and a legislator involved in parliamentary relations with France, said Kyiv was worried about any pro-Russian agenda but was not actively preparing for a Le Pen victory.Oleksandr Merezhko, head of Ukraine's parliamentary foreign affairs committee, said French lawmakers had assured him that even if Le Pen won, she would not act against France's institutions or national interests. articles.title: Emma Barnett: Host to leave Radio 4's Today and start new BBC Show
articles.summary: Barnett, who has presented Today and Woman's Hour, will front a multiplatform show in the New Year.
articles.body:
Radio 4 presenter Emma Barnett is set to leave the Today programme this week for a multiplatform new BBC show in the New Year.

Former Woman's Hour host Barnett has developed a "bold" new show, she says, which will launch in 2027 across BBC Sounds, BBC iPlayer and YouTube.

Her final day presenting Radio 4's flagship morning news and current affairs show will be on Wednesday 18 November.

"For the last nearly six years - it's been incredible to talk to the mighty Radio 4 listeners," she said in a statement. "Having proudly hosted Woman's Hour and now the Today Programme - I've had the rare pleasure of hosting nearly every hour of the morning on this truly unique and special radio network."

She added: "But it's not goodbye to the BBC audience I value so greatly because I have something else for them that I hope will add something meaningful and entertaining to their lives."

Posting on Instagram , she said there would be more information on what her new show would be about soon.

"Watch this space and look ready. I am… More soon."

Barnett joined Today in May 2024, taking over from Martha Kearney to work alongside co-presenters Nick Robinson, Mishal Husain, Amol Rajan and Justin Webb. Husain and Rajan have since left.

Today programme editor Rebecca Keating said Barnett had brought "enormous energy" to Today, with "a keen focus" on listeners.

She noted how Barnett had a proven "track record of telling stories of personal hardship that influence public debate" but how she was "also equally at home interviewing British icons like Dame Judi Dench.

"We will miss her generous tea making and wish her every success in her new venture."

In August, Barnett, 41, revealed she had had a hysterectomy and surgery for endometriosis, days before a documentary she made about the condition was broadcast.

She returned to the Today programme explaining she had been absent in recent weeks because she was in hospital "in a case of life imitating work".

Speaking on her BBC podcast, Ready to Talk with Emma Barnett, last year, she told listeners that finding out she was going through perimenopause at the age of 38 felt like she had been "mugged, robbed".

The broadcaster said it was the "first time in my life I haven't really wanted to be a woman - it's the first time I've thought, I'd really quite like to be a bloke".

Radio 4 controller Mohit Bakaya said he was "delighted she's staying with the BBC" and would "look forward to her new show."
